thumbnails.desc: This virtual reality project was made for my Masters thesis at Purdue University. Everything (except the 3D models) was made from scratch. The basic idea was to develop a system that could quickly synthesize a multi-character scenario (which can be extrapolated to crowds), with each character having their own levels of 'perceived negative emotion by the player' (a.k.a. affect). Each character came with proxemics logic that enabled them to have a concept of personal space. This project also demonstrated how to optimize this scenario using Simulated Annealing, so that the algorithm can adjust itself towards a target 'overall negative affect' of the scene.

Pictured above is the final setup of the characters - optimized for a target value of negative affect (emotion). The characters walk from these points to the player's position, as the player 'walks' the street.
An example of a female character displaying 'no-look at' and 'look-at' behavior.
The main script for a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method called Simulated Annealing.
Flowchart of the overall experiement.

cardsTab1.title: Blockrun (Unreal Engine)
cardsTab1.desc: Singleplayer & Multiplayer Adventure and Puzzle Solving

thumbnails.desc: Singleplayer - Adventure game where the point is to collect coins and keys to open a map area to start a minigame where you have to play tetris in a smart way to form a bridge, so that you can help the penguins cross the lave lake its over.

The Tetromino Creation Lab. Here the player (Adventurer role) will be able to create their own tetromino shapes dynamically and use those during the tetris minigame to be used to complete it. In the multiplayer setup, the adventurer will create the shapes and if the Puzzle Solver is also in the same minigame room, the created tetromino can be sent to the puzzle solver in-real time. So, in case a non-traditional tetromino shape is needed, the players can communicate and get the correct shape. This is done to promote collaborative puzzle solving.

A completed tetris minigame, where a 'bridge' has been made for the penguins to cross. There are a certain number of penguins that need to be saved and if they don't see a path in front of them, they are killed off and the player loses points. The red surface is supposed to be lava. The green objects are the penguins.

Multiplayer - on the left the host (Puzzle Solver role) starts the server. On the right the client can join in a lobby supporting 5 players max. The multiplayer lobby settings are configurable and so are the character colors. The code automatically assigns the other player as the Adventurer.
Two player session with Puzzle Solver and Adventurer.
Another feature is only the player (usually the Adventurer role) that holds the key can open the door (other players can see the door but it will appear 'Locked' to them).

Animations and actor objects are synced across the network. Here the Adventurer sees the Puzzle solver go in and start the tetris minigame with the default tetrominos. At this point the Adventurer can go to the Tetromino Creation Room and create shapes to send to the Puzzle Solver.
Flowchart of the entire game logic.
Flowcharts depicting the logic for each of the minigame subsystems (Puzzle Solving Tetris miniagem and Tetromino Creation Lab subsystem)
As a research component, a diegetic feedback screen was added after the completion of the Puzzle Solver's Tetris minigame to collect feedback.

cardsTab1.title: Traits Extension to Schelling's Segregation Model
cardsTab1.desc: Extending Schelling's Segregation model by comparing similarity of trait vectors

thumbnails.desc: This research presented a preliminary exploration into traits-based extension of Schelling's Model of Segregation. Two simulations were developed and compared for agent behavior and dynamics- the Multi-Agent Schelling Model (MASM) and the High-Dimensional Personality Schelling Model (HDPSM). Better images will be available soon.

Interface for setting parameters for HDPSM. This enabled five different types of population, each with their own unique dominant trait based personality vector. Even within a population, each individual agent had slight variation in their personality as well.

The HDPSM running in two agent types mode, which effectively turns it into the Classical Schelling's Model (CSM). The method was able to preserve the expected behavior of the CSM, thus providing significant evidence towards the success of this approach.

Display's the Morans I Spatial Distribution map of Agent A, after testing for significance. Clustered behavior is also as expected of the CSM, thus ensuring that the arrangement patterns were not just by random chance. (Red = HH, Light Red = HL, Light Blue = LH, Blue = LL)

Display's the Morans I Spatial Distribution map of Agent B. Notice that it is an 'inverted' map of the Moran's I map of Agent A (since this is a two agent system). (Red = HH, Light Red = HL, Light Blue = LH, Blue = LL)

Multi agent simualtion where each agent displays a run-hide-fight decision-making mechanic. The idea is that when a threat comes into a safezone, based on the characteristics of the blue colored agent, they can either choose to stay and hide, run away, or run towards threat and fight. The color of the agent denotes their state.

The user's mouse controls a 'threat', the green circles are safezones - each with its own max capacity, and the blue squares are agents that each have their own preference towards addressing a threat and have their own comfort level with how many people are around them.
An example simulation where a red-colored fight agent is seeking out the threat to actively take it down.
Safe spots can detect all non-threat agents in range. The red lines (yellow lines seen previously) are just debug lines to calculate distance of the threat from that safezone.

The non-threat agent's decision making logic. At the end, they either choose and commit to running away to a new safezone, staying and hiding in the current safezone, or running towards the threat to take it down.
The underlying Neuroticism (from Five Factor Model) equation that dictates the agent's neuroticism level that determines how they perceive the threat and how they respond to it.
The agent's script that contains all logic of neuroticism. The boolean flags array works as a state machine.

This is a conceptual behavioral diagram I created based on how the societal balance is being upheld by its constituent's needs being satisfied, which in turn upholds the three pillars of societal sustenance. If there is an imbalance in needs, then the balance is off, which means that society will focus unequally on one of the three pillars of sustenance (in this case the social pillar since the divide among the constituents contributes to major societal problems). As a result, progress will be skewed towards that component while the other pillars might be addressed with a regressive mindset.

cardsTab1.desc: Cellular Automata & MANTIS based projects for Ph.D. Dissertation

thumbnails.desc: Modular Conway's Game of Life experiment, where rule values can be changed real time to study cellular automata behavior. Here is an example configuration where the shape was very square-based and only expanded from the corners. Conditions were: Underpopulation = 1, Survival = [3,4], Overpopulation = 4, Reproduction = 1
This was one of the setups that produced an ever expanding organic 'brain-like' shape. Conditions were: Underpopulation = 2, Survival = [2,3], Overpopulation = 4, Reproduction = 3
More images will be available after publication is printed.

Worked with Iconic Engine's in-house SDK (Vasoo Engine) to develop a metaverse sports experience for the Oculus Quest. I was a Project Manager and Lead Mechanics Developer for the Interior Experience team, whose goal was to create a skybox area for multiple avatars to hang out, watch the actual match, and have social interactions with other users.
The outdoor stadium developed by the Outdoor Experience team. I assisted with level design for both teams as well as code integration, and documentation.
An aerial view of the final experience with the outdoor stadium and the indoor 'lounge' area.

cardsTab1.title: Diegetic vs. Minimap VR Navigation (Unity)
cardsTab1.desc: Diegetic navigation aid against traditional 2D (in-world) minimap for VR navigation

thumbnails.desc: Developed a virtual reality simulation that focused on comparing the enjoyment levels, ease of use, and usability of diegetic (in-world user-interfaces) navigational aids compared to traditional minimaps. In this image, the player can only open the gate if their “card” credentials match that gate's lock combination.

The minimap provides a top-down view of the entire map (player in pink and destination in yellow). The map is a simple texture on a plane object and has no signs of being an in-world object (non-diegetic).
Game view that shows the eye-level POV of the player. This environment is meant to evoke the feeling of being in the streets of a crowded city with many alleys and cul-de-sacs.
Diegetic mode shows if correct key is inserted.
Diegetic mode shows if incorrect key is inserted.
Top-down view of the map displaying the layout of the world. During gameplay, it displays the player's realtime location and the destination as well.

cardsTab2.title: Collection Quest (Unity)
cardsTab2.desc: VR Simulation & NPC Intelligence System Design

thumbnails.desc: AI Patrol Agents for a game (used for a published article) that move between 'n' checkpoints randomly to simulate enemy guard behavior. The agent also comes with a player detection zone (light blue zone using a sphere-overlap), to simulate enemy chase behavior.

Once the player enters the detection zone (light blue), the patrol agent notices the player and starts following it, overriding the checkpoint patrol behavior. The zone also turns black indicating that the player is seen, and the agent will follow with a slightly higher speed, until the player comes out of the detection zone.

Grid visibility detection script used in a game level for a published article. Here the level was optimized for the location of multiple pieces of a treasure. The factors were several cost terms (one of which was 'initial visibility of the player'). The tiles in red are the ones that have detected the yellow treasure  (high visibility). Since it is inside a room (white blocks), the green tiles do not 'see' it, thus implementing an effective visibility algorithm.

The primary focus was to understand the mechanics behind the design of video games without the help of a game engine, by recreating elements of a classic video game. Some of the fundamental concepts explored were keyboard inputs for gameplay, GLSL Shader coding, Non-Photorealistic Rendering (that function as power-up effects, collisions between elements, and basic fundamental game mechanics. Levels consisted of unbreakable blocks and enemies. Each type of enemy when destroyed drops a power-up.

Power-up 1 activated (Chaos mode - where the screen moves around changing perspective). An interesting by-product of this mode was the changed appearance of the enemies due to changing the shader buffers (which was a happy and unexpected accident).
Power-up 2 activated (Inversion - Turns the game upside down).
Win screen.

cardsTab2.title: Procedurally Generated Infinite Dungeon Sidescroller
cardsTab2.desc: Game that creates procedural dungeons and repeats the chunks for an endless sidescroller.

thumbnails.desc: This project covered the development of an infinite sidescroller, where the “level” chunks are generated procedurally. These chunks behave as pooled objects that always number in three (i.e. after the second dungeon chunk is cleared, the third one acts as the first in the next series of three.
Each dungeon in a chunk is comprised of a gridlike system which is always optimized for one escape route. All dungeons are randomized and procedural.
Gameplay screenshot of a player traversing the dungeon 'terrain' and on top the chunks can be seen.

Fully procedural seating generator. The user just needs to click on the generate button (and set the starter parameters on the left if they wish to) and everytime, a new form of sittable furniture will be generated.

One feature this algorithm also has is the edge (red blocks) and corner (yellow blocks without the grey pegs) detection abilities of the base, thus making it very versatile, and providing with the ability to generate any form of seats (from ottomans to sofas to barstools).

cardsTab2.title: Crime Visualizer and Detective Game (Unity)
cardsTab2.desc: Data Parser and Data-Driven Game Design

thumbnails.desc: A small game was developed that mapped all the points over approximately correct geographic locations (over a map image). The player could then click on each green 'hotspot' and look into the details of the homicide that happened in that area.
Main play screen ('PLAY' state); The red hat is the player icon, and the green marks are the crime 'hotspots' containing the information from the dataset.

Clicking on a location puts the game in the 'INSPECT' state reveals the details about the crime there and the player can play a sound byte from that location to see if it matches with the culprit or not.
An example of a hint given to the player (the information in the curly brackets is supposed to be what the hint alludes to).
If the user successfully finds the location with the same sound clip as given in the clue. If the user is unsuccessful in finding the correct location with the same sound clip as given in the clue.

A small game was developed that mapped all the points over approximately correct geographic locations (over a map image). The player could then click on each green 'hotspot' and look into the details of the homicide that happened in that area.

cardsTab2.title: Knowledge Management of Video Game Postmortems
cardsTab2.desc: An exploration into developing a novel visualization for game postmortems

thumbnails.desc: An example of the end result of the methodology of taking a video game's postmortem, vectorizing it, and reducing the dimensions to major problem spaces.

The proposed process where after vectorization and tokenizing, a wordy postmortem can be reduced in terms of how it is represented (with minimal additions for context) and still preserve the information communicated by the original postmortem.
A sie-by-side comparison between using the same vectorization and plotting technique for the original postmortem and the reduced postmortem text.

This virtual reality demo was created as a part of the edX course I did, entitled “Creating Virtual Reality Applications” (UCSanDiegoX:CSE190x). A major focus was to build a 'one-button' system for virtual reality based environments. The application comprises of two parts - creation of game objects in a virtual room and manipulating them (along with existing objects in the scene). The user is able to freely create objects and them relocate, rotate, and scale them, using three different modes of locomotion - teleport, walk, and an automatic hover mode. Diegetic menu for instantiating items was also implemented
All items in the level are rigidbodies, which enables the player to interact with them.
A minimap also exists to display a top down view of the room.
An object highlight feature is also implemented. If the raycast from the player detects a rigidbody with a custom tag, the algorithm applies a red overlay on top of it, to indicate context.
One of my first dives into virtual reality game development (2018). However, this was back when I did not have access to proper equipment, thus having to make this 'one-button controller' simulation.

A project I made to harnesses the power of hand tracking that is provided by Oculus Quest. A major focus of the application was to implement pose recognition. The user is able to set custom gestures, and spawn in objects, and interact with them. Some of the implemented features are custom pose setup, pose recognition, use gesture to 'force call' objects towards player and 'force blast' it away, physics interaction with environment elements (springs, rigidbodies, buttons etc.), and it all comes together in a minigame, where the player has to blast the ball towards a randomly generated target on the wall for points.
There was also a minigame included where players could make objects float (using one hand sign) and then blast them towards a target to score points (using another hand sign).
The player stood in front of physics accurate buttons, that could be used to record custom poses, and map them to custom functions.

A virtual reality game I worked on for the CGT 555 (Game Development II) class, at Purdue University for my Masters. I fulfilled the role as a Creative Director and Level Designer (for 3 out of the 4 levels). This was also the start of Hammerand Studios - the starting point of having my own game development team. Topplots puts you in the shoes of a young child whose sole aim is to take down the towers of blocks in front of them, to get to the unique toys at the top of it. Take charge and gradually advance to locations that will take you on a wild journey fueled by the child's imagination. The images represent the levels I worked on.
Underworld (Level 3)- playspace in the middle is marked with the white and red mat.
Mole World (Level 2) - playspace is in the mesa in the middle.

A level design project, that primarily focuses on environment design. Primary goals were to work with foliage (LoD levels) and terrain design tools, as well as lighting scenarions. It also includes a log cabin, as well as smoke and fire particle effects. The First Person Shooter template of Unreal Engine has been used here, to allow the player to roam about, and experience the environment. Natural vegetation is prevalent in this 4 KM x 4 KM world.
Rock formations were manually placed, and oriented.
The cabin is an Unreal Marketplace asset. The campfire includes particle effects and sound.
The aesthetic was made to mimic classic 'lost in the forest' style games, that displayed themes of horror and solitary survivalism.
As you look into the woods, maybe something looks back?

A level design project created using assets from Quixel Megascans. The idea here was to generate a small settlement, surrounded by rocky mountains, in a desolate area. The main theme of the level design is to create a semi-fantasy based habitation area, and night time was chosen for aesthetic appeal.
A peaceful village called 'Oasis' on the edge of an asteroid.
Main focus was to integrate Quixel Megascans assets into the world, for a linear game level.
The level design was done by hand. The layout follows closely with a place I am very familiar with. Terrain manipulation and heightmaps were generated using World Machine.
To make the scene more interesting, a night scene was decided on. Along with that, the lamps are custom blueprints, and the trees have wind animations built in.

cardsTab4.title: Assignment Requirement Document Template
cardsTab4.desc: Standardized template for classroom assignment (ADA Compliant)

thumbnails.desc: This template was developed for using in Manufacturing Engineering Technology classes that I TA for. Feel free to use this template as a starting point when creating your documents. Features include compartmentalization between assignment steps and resources, visual sectioning to guide readers, organized silos for functional information, and table based grid layout.

cardsTab4.title: Assignment and Project Grading Tool
cardsTab4.desc: Unity based tool to create a grading tool from .txt data sources

thumbnails.desc: Grading tool separates regular assignments (with just rubric items) and projects (contains multi-level rubric items). The data gets pre-loaded before the grading interface loads, thus making grading faster and more responsive.

Graders can select from a lost of assignments (same goes for project). Instructors can follow the syntax of the assignments data file to populate this list. They can also add custom rubric items, as long as the correct rubric item ID is mentioned.

The grading screen with rubric gets auto generated based on the data source. The base shell generates the assignment specific screen during runtime and all score manipulation and feedback generation is done real time. If the score obtained is less than the total score of the rubric iten, the background of the element changes color to indicate a change has been made. The Total Score also updates real time.

The project grading screen builds upon the regular assignment grading shell, however since the project has multiple levels of data, the grader can switch between all the components and grade each individually. The feedback format also changes and tracks each level's feedback. The buttons are also generated real time, since the data is already preloaded.

An example of what the feedback looks like for the project. Each line contains the Level 0 data (Assembly), Level 1 data (Part), and Level 2 data (rubric item) as well as the deduction. Once the Copy Feedback button is pressed, it auto copies this formatted feedback to the clipboard, so the grader only needs to paste it into the appropriate place in the Learning Management System.
The current iteration of the tool uses three data sources, each as a TXT file (data is stored as CSV). The ID is used as the Primary Key to establish links in between the sources.
